segments.title: Why proximity to events shapes source ranking
segments.body: Historians rank sources by how far they are removed from the event under study. An eyewitness account or an official document compiled at the time by participants counts as primary evidence in this framework. It preserves their observations and memories more directly than a later compilation, though every account remains partial. Primary, secondary, and tertiary describe a source's relationship to events, so the rank does not make any one version the whole truth.

evidence.note: The transcript defines source ranks by their removal from an event and describes contemporary eyewitness accounts and official documents as primary.

segments.summary: Primary, secondary, and tertiary identify how far a source is removed from events, with primary evidence closest to participants and contemporary records.
segments.question: Why do historians prioritize primary sources and rank evidence as primary, secondary, or tertiary?
segments.answerShort: Because source ranks describe distance from the event: firsthand accounts and contemporary documents preserve participants' observations and memories most directly.

segments.title: Jutland reports show why versions matter
segments.body: The Jutland reporting example shows how a secondary compilation can reshape primary information. The original material says one thing, while the published report says another. The officer whose account was blocked then issues the earlier version as a book, partly because the ordered rewrite has impugned his honor. Comparing the two versions exposes disagreement, institutional pressure, and the personal stakes behind an official record.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts original Jutland information with a published report and describes an officer publishing an earlier report after it was blocked.

segments.summary: The Jutland example shows how an original account, an official published report, and a later book can preserve competing versions of the same event.

segments.title: Reconstructing a battle from different viewpoints
segments.body: Tertiary work is a historian's synthesis built from primary and secondary material. A sailor in a ship's engine room and someone in the gun director experience the same battle from different positions, which shapes what each observes and concludes. Neither perspective alone can reconstruct the engagement. Historians compare as many accounts as possible and set them in context to build a fuller picture of what happened. Source grades identify how close the evidence is to the event, while corroboration shows how separate accounts fit together.

evidence.note: The transcript defines tertiary work, then explains that historians compare contrasting perspectives such as those from an engine room and a gun director.

segments.summary: A historian's synthesis grows from comparing partial firsthand perspectives, such as those of an engine-room sailor and a gun-director crew during the same battle.
